On the Correlations between Galaxy Properties and Supermassive Black Hole Mass

On the Correlations between Galaxy Properties and Supermassive Black Hole Mass–62011
A.  Beifiori ††thanks: E-mail:beifiori@mpe.mpg.de Affiliation: Max-Planck-Institut für Extraterrestrische Physik, Giessenbachstraße, D-85748 Garching, Germany Affiliation: Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation, Dennis Sciama Building, Burnaby Road, Portsmouth, PO1 3FX, United Kingdom    S. Courteau Affiliation: Queen’s University, Department of Physics, Engineering Physics and Astronomy, Kingston, ON, K7L 3N6, Canada    E. M. Corsini Affiliation: Dipartimento di Astronomia, Università di Padova, vicolo dell’Osservatorio 3, I-35122 Padova, Italy    Y. Accepted 2011 September 27. Received 2011 September 13; in original form 2011 January 5
Abstract

We use a large sample of upper limits and accurate estimates of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) masses coupled with libraries of host galaxy velocity dispersions, rotational velocities and photometric parameters extracted from Sloan Digital Sky Survey ii-band images to establish correlations between the SMBH and host galaxy parameters. We test whether the mass of the black hole, M∙M_{\bullet}, is fundamentally driven by either local or global galaxy properties. We explore correlations between M∙M_{\bullet} and stellar velocity dispersion σe\sigma_{\rm e}, ii-band bulge luminosity Li,bulgeL_{i,{\rm bulge}}, bulge mass MbulgeM_{\rm bulge}, bulge Sérsic index nn, bulge mean effective surface brightness ⟨μe,bulge⟩\langle\mu_{\rm e,bulge}\rangle, ii-band luminosity of the galaxy Li,galL_{i,{\rm gal}}, galaxy stellar mass M⋆,galM_{\star,\rm gal}, maximum circular velocity VcV_{\rm c}, galaxy dynamical and effective masses Mdyn,galM_{\rm dyn,gal} and Me,galM_{\rm e,gal}. We verify the tightness of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation and find that correlations with other galaxy parameters do not yield tighter trends. We do not find differences in the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation of barred and unbarred galaxies. The M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation of pseudo-bulges is also coarser and has a different slope than that involving classical bulges. The M∙M_{\bullet}−-MbulgeM_{\rm bulge} is not as tight as the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation, despite the bulge mass proving to be a better proxy of M∙M_{\bullet} than bulge luminosity, and despite adding the bulge effective radius as an additional fitting parameter. Contrary to various published reports, we find a rather poor correlation between M∙M_{\bullet} and nn (or ⟨μe,bulge⟩\langle\mu_{\rm e,bulge}\rangle) suggesting that M∙M_{\bullet} is not related to the bulge light concentration. The correlations between M∙M_{\bullet} and galaxy luminosity or mass are not a marked improvement over the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation. These scaling relations depend sensitively on the host galaxy morphology: early-type galaxies follow a tighter relation than late-type galaxies. If VcV_{\rm c} is a proxy for the dark matter halo mass, the large scatter of the M∙−VcM_{\bullet}-V_{\rm c} relation then suggests that M∙M_{\bullet} is more coupled to the baryonic rather than the dark matter. We have tested the need for a third parameter in the M∙M_{\bullet} scaling relations, through various linear correlations with bulge and galaxy parameters, only to confirm that the fundamental plane of the SMBH is mainly driven by σe\sigma_{\rm e}  with a small tilt due to the effective radius. We provide a compendium of galaxy structural properties for most of the SMBH hosts known to date.

Keywords: 
black holes physics — galaxies: fundamental parameters — galaxies: photometry — galaxies: kinematics and dynamics — galaxies: statistics

1 Introduction

The mass M∙M_{\bullet} of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) is closely tied to the properties of the spheroidal component of galaxies, such as the bulge luminosity, LbulgeL_{\rm bulge} (Dressler, 1989; Kormendy & Richstone, 1995; Marconi & Hunt, 2003; Graham, 2007; Gültekinet al., 2009, hereafter 66), the stellar velocity dispersion, σ\sigma (Ferrarese & Merritt 2000; Gebhardt et al. 2000; Tremaine et al. 2002; Ferrarese & Ford 2005; 66), the mass of the bulge (Magorrian et al., 1998; Häring & Rix, 2004), the central light concentration (Graham et al., 2001), the Sérsic index (Graham & Driver, 2007), the virial mass of the galaxy (Ferrarese et al., 2006), the gravitational binding energy (Aller & Richstone, 2007), the kinetic energy of random motions of the bulge (Feoli & Mancini, 2009), and the stellar light and mass deficit associated to the core ellipticals (Lauer et al., 2007; Kormendy & Bender, 2009). Most of these relations are inter-compared in Novak et al. (2006) and in 66. Given the M∙−σM_{\bullet}-\sigma relation and the correlation between σ\sigma and the circular velocity, VcV_{\rm c}, Ferrarese (2002) and Pizzella et al. (2005) suggested a link between M∙M_{\bullet} and VcV_{\rm c} (or equivalently, with the mass of the dark matter halo). However, Courteau et al. (2007) and Ho (2007) pointed out that the VcV_{\rm c}−-σ\sigma relation actually depends on galaxy morphology (or equivalently, on its light concentration) thus precluding a simple connection between M∙M_{\bullet} and VcV_{\rm c}. Kormendy & Bender (2011) studied a sample of bulgeless galaxies and concluded that there is almost no correlation between the SMBH and dark matter halo, unless the galaxy also contains a bulge.

Several authors have noted that the residuals of the M∙−σM_{\bullet}-\sigma and M∙−LbulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm bulge} relations correlate with the galaxy effective radius (Marconi & Hunt, 2003, e.g.,). Hopkins et al. (2007a); Hopkins et al. (2007b) suggested the possibility of a linear combination between different galaxy properties to reduce the scatter of the M∙M_{\bullet} scaling laws, heralding the idea of a fundamental plane of SMBHs (BHFP). Many SMBH scaling relations could thus be seen as projections of the BHFP (Aller & Richstone, 2007; Barway & Kembhavi, 2007). A correlation of M∙M_{\bullet} with more than one galaxy parameter would suggest a SMBH growth sensitive to the overall structure of the host galaxy.

The local characterisation and cosmic evolution of the M∙M_{\bullet} scaling relations have already been examined through theoretical models for the coevolution of galaxies and SMBHs (Granato et al., 2004; Vittorini et al., 2005; Hopkins et al., 2006; Monaco et al., 2007). These studies have revealed that the observed scaling relations could be reproduced in models of SMBH growth with strong feedback from the active galactic nucleus (Silk & Rees, 1998; Cox et al., 2006; Robertson et al., 2006a; Robertson et al., 2006b; Di Matteo et al., 2005, AGN,). In particular, these models predict the existence of the BHFP (Hopkins et al., 2007a; Hopkins et al., 2007b; Hopkins et al., 2009). However, while the observed relations can be reproduced by the models, these still depend on the adopted slope, zero point, and scatter (Somerville, 2009) which remain ill-constrained.

In this work, we make use of a large sample of galaxies with available M∙M_{\bullet} estimates to improve our understanding of the known scaling laws over a wide range of M∙M_{\bullet}, morphological type and nuclear activity, as well as to test for possible correlations of M∙M_{\bullet} with different combinations of spheroid and galaxy parameters.

This paper is organised as follows. The sample of SMBH hosts is described in §2. Their photometric, kinematic, and dynamical properties are presented in §3, while the correlations between M∙M_{\bullet} and the bulge and galaxy properties are shown in §4. We discuss our results and conclude in §5.

2 Sample Description

The M∙M_{\bullet} values were retrieved from two different samples: the compilation of M∙M_{\bullet} upper limits by Beifiori et al. (2009, hereafter B09 ) and the compilation of secure M∙M_{\bullet} by 66.

The M∙M_{\bullet} estimates of 12 were obtained from Hubble Space Telescope (HST) archival spectra. That sample includes nuclear spectra for 105 nearby galaxies with D<100D<100 Mpc obtained with the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) equipped with the G750M grating. The spectra cover the region of the Hα\alpha line and [N ii]λ​λ​6548,6583\,\lambda\lambda 6548,6583 and [S ii]λ​λ​6716,6731\,\lambda\lambda 6716,6731 doublets. The nebular-line widths were modelled in terms of gas motion in a thin disc of unknown orientation but known spatial extent following the method of Sarzi et al. (2002). 12 adopted two different inclinations for the gaseous disc with a nearly face-on disc (i=33i=33∘) hosting a larger M∙M_{\bullet} and a nearly edge-on disc (81∘) harbouring a smaller M∙M_{\bullet}. The two inclinations correspond to the 68% upper and lower confidence limits for randomly oriented discs. We augmented the 12 sample with the M∙M_{\bullet} upper limits of NGC 2892 and NGC 5921. The STIS/G750M spectra for these galaxies were retrieved from the HST archive and we have calculated their M∙M_{\bullet} upper limits from the nebular line widths following the prescription of 12. We include in Sample A the set of 105 galaxies from 12 minus 18 galaxies in common with 66 (15 of them with a secure M∙M_{\bullet} and 3 with a M∙M_{\bullet} upper limit derived from the dynamical modelling of resolved kinematics). We are left with 87 M∙M_{\bullet} upper limits from 12 based on nebular-line widths. We also include two newly determined M∙M_{\bullet} upper limits and the five upper limits derived from the dynamical modelling of resolved kinematics by 66. The resulting 94 galaxies constitute our Sample A.

66 collected M∙M_{\bullet} data published up to November 2008 based on the resolved kinematics of ionised gas, stars, and water maser for total sample of 49 galaxies with a secure M∙M_{\bullet} estimate and 18 galaxies with a M∙M_{\bullet} upper limit. Our Sample B is limited to the 49 definite values of M∙M_{\bullet}. The five upper limits derived from the dynamical modelling of resolved kinematics already belong to Sample A. The remaining 13 upper limits by 66 are taken from the nebular line width measurements by Sarzi et al. (2002). They were also measured by 12 and are therefore already included in Sample A.

All the data relative to Samples A and B are listed in Table 1 and 2, respectively. The upper limits by 12 were rescaled assuming H0=70H_{0}=70 km​s−1​Mpc−1\mathrm{km\;s^{-1}\;Mpc^{-1}}, Ωm=0.3\Omega_{\rm m}=0.3, and ΩΛ=0.7\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.7 to conform with 66.

Figure 1 shows the upper limits and the accurate determinations of M∙M_{\bullet} for the 18 galaxies in common between the 12 and 66 samples. The M∙M_{\bullet} estimates by 12 and 66 are consistent within 1​σ1\sigma of each other; no systematic offset is detected. Thus, nebular line width measurements by 12 (included in Sample A) trace well the nuclear gravitational potential dominated by the central SMBH, allowing a reliable estimate of M∙M_{\bullet} (as those in Sample B). Therefore, we shall use the M∙M_{\bullet} upper limits from Sample A to study the correlations of M∙M_{\bullet} versus various galaxy parameters. We adopt for our tests the case of i=33i=33∘ which maximises the upper limit on M∙M_{\bullet}. 12 already compared their M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation with those of Ferrarese & Ford (2005) and Lauer et al. (2007) to show that their upper limits on M∙M_{\bullet} (included in Sample A) are a valuable proxy for the more secure determinations of M∙M_{\bullet} (comprised in Sample B). A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on the distributions of M∙M_{\bullet} and σ\sigma indicates that Samples A and B could be drawn from the same parent distribution to better than the 80% confidence level. For this reason, we merged Samples A and B into a joint A++B data set. The combination of Samples A and B yields a total sample of 143 M∙M_{\bullet} determinations. The union of those two samples proves most valuable for the proper statistical assessment of scaling relations with M∙M_{\bullet}.

3 Galaxy Properties

The aim of this study is to determine the strength of the correlations, if any, between M∙M_{\bullet} and the properties of their host galaxies. For the latter, we have compiled as large a collection as possible of homogeneous measurements of photometric parameters (effective radius, effective surface brightness, Sérsic index, and luminosity of the bulge, effective radius, effective surface brightness, concentration, and total luminosity of the galaxy), kinematic properties (stellar velocity dispersion and circular velocity), and masses (bulge mass, galaxy stellar mass, virial and dynamical mass of the galaxy).

The sample demographics are as follows: 29% of the host galaxies are ellipticals, 27% lenticulars, and 44% are spirals (de Vaucouleurs et al., 1991, hereafter RC3). Regarding nuclear activity, 23% of the sample galaxies are Low-Ionisation Nuclear Emission-line Regions (LINERs), 11% host H ii nuclei, 25% are Seyferts, and 8% are classified as transition objects according to Ho et al. (1997). The remaining 33% do not show central emission.

We describe in the sub-sections below the extraction of all the galaxy structural parameters.

3.1 Galaxy Photometric Parameters

We retrieved gg and ii-band images from the seventh data release (Abazajian et al., 2009, DR7,) of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (York et al., 2000, SDSS,) for as many Sample A and B galaxies as possible. The total SDSS sample includes 90 galaxies, 62 from Sample A and 28 from Sample B, from which to derive structural parameters.

The SDSS images are already bias subtracted, flat-fielded and cleaned from bright stars; however, we performed our own sky subtraction since the SDSS pipeline sky levels may be flawed for extended galaxies (Bernardi et al., 2007; Lauer et al., 2007). This issue has been addressed in the SDSS-III Data Release 8 (Aihara et al., 2011; Blanton et al., 2011). For our purposes, we estimated the sky level of each galaxy image by isolating five regions away from the galaxy, free of any contaminant, and calculating the mode of the sky intensities per pixel within each sky region. The average and standard deviation of the five sky values was then computed. The difference between our measured sky values and those provided by SDSS can be as large as 4%4\%. The SDSS sky level is always biased high, likely due to the inclusion of bright, extended sources while our interactive technique ensures a contaminant-free selection of the sky fields. We find that the typical surface brightness error in the gg and ii bands is 0.1 mag arcsec-2 at μg≃26\mu_{g}\simeq 26 mag arcsec-2 and μi≃25\mu_{i}\simeq 25 mag arcsec-2, respectively (see McDonald et al., 2011, for more details). The large angular extent of NGC 224 and NGC 4594 relative to the field of view thwarted their proper sky subtraction; these two galaxies were therefore excluded from our SDSS sample. NGC 221 was also discarded due to improper positioning of the image on the detector. The remaining images were flux-calibrated based on the SDSS photometric zero-point, corrected for Galactic extinction (Schlegel et al., 1998) as well as for internal extinction and KK-correction following Shao et al. (2007).

The galaxy surface brightness profiles were extracted using the isophotal fitting methods outlined in Courteau et al. (1996) and McDonald et al. (2011). These make use of the astronomical data reduction package XVISTA11 1 See http://astronomy.nmsu.edu/holtz/xvista/index.html.. The azimuthally-averaged surface brightness profiles, projected onto the major axis of each galaxy, are shown in Figure 2 for four sample galaxies. These are the elliptical galaxy NGC 5127, two high- (NGC 4036) and low- (NGC 4477) inclination lenticular galaxies, and the spiral galaxy NGC 3675 which boasts a remarkably high dust content.

The gg and ii-band total magnitude of each galaxy is then determined by summing the flux at each isophote and extrapolating the light profile to infinity. The g−ig-i colour of each galaxy was calculated from the difference of the fully corrected gg and ii-band magnitudes. The remaining structural parameters were measured from the ii-band light profiles since, of all the SDSS band passes, the ii-band suffers least dust extinction. We extracted the isophotal radius, r24.5r_{24.5}, corresponding to the surface brightness of 24.5 mag arcsec-2, the half-light (or effective) radius of the galaxy, re,galr_{\rm e,gal}, the effective surface brightness of the galaxy, μe,gal\mu_{\rm e,gal}, and the galaxy concentration C28=5​log⁡(r80/r20)C_{28}=5\log(r_{80}/r_{20}), where r20r_{20} and r80r_{80} are the radii which enclose 20%20\% and 80%80\% of the total luminosity, respectively. These ii-band structural parameters are listed in Table 3. The gg-band magnitude is also listed. Based on simulated models of spiral galaxies (MacArthur et al., 2003), the typical error per galaxy structural parameter is roughly 10-20%.

3.2 Photometric Parameters of Bulges and Discs

The structural parameters for elliptical galaxies, modelled typically as a single spheroid, and for spiral galaxies, modelled as the sum of a spheroid and a disc, were derived by applying the two-dimensional photometric decomposition algorithm GASP2D (Méndez-Abreu et al., 2008) to the SDSS i−i-band images.

The surface brightness of the spheroid component (typically the entire elliptical galaxy or the bulge component for a disc galaxy) is modelled using a Sérsic function (Sérsic 1968; see also Graham & Driver 2005)

Ib​(r)=Ie​10−bn​{(r/re)1/n−1},I_{\rm b}(r)=I_{\rm e}10^{-b_{n}\{\left(r/r_{\rm e}\right)^{1/n}-1\}}, (1)

where rer_{\rm e} is the effective radius, IeI_{\rm e} is the surface brightness at rer_{\rm e} , and nn is a shape parameter that describes the curvature of the radial profile. With n=1n=1 or n=4n=4, the Sérsic function reduces to the exponential or de Vaucouleurs function, respectively. The coefficient bn=0.868​n−0.142b_{n}=0.868\,n-0.142 (Caon et al., 1993) is a normalisation term. The spheroid model elliptical isophotes have constant position angle PAb and constant axial ratio qbq_{\rm b}.

The surface brightness distribution of the disc component is assumed to follow an exponential law (Freeman, 1970)

Id(r)=I0e−r/h,I_{\rm d}(r)=I_{0}\,{\rm e}^{-r/h}, (2)

where hh and I0I_{0} are the scale length and central surface brightness of the disc, respectively. The disc model elliptical isophotes have constant position angle PAd and constant axial ratio qdq_{\rm d}. The fitting algorithm GASP2D relies on a χ2\chi^{2} minimisation of the intensities in counts, for which we must adopt initial trial parameters that are as close as possible to their final values. The latter were estimated from our ellipse-averaged light profiles from which basic fits to the bulge and disc were applied to estimate structural parameters (see Méndez-Abreu et al., 2008, for details). The χ2\chi^{2} minimisation is based on the robust Levenberg-Marquardt method by Moré et al. (1980). The actual computation has been done using the MPFIT algorithm (Markwardt, 2009) under the IDL22 2 Interactive Data Language is distributed by ITT Visual Information Solutions. It is available from http://www.ittvis.com/. environment.

The GASP2D software yields structural parameters for the bulge (IeI_{\rm e}, rer_{\rm e}, nn, PAb, and qbq_{\rm b}) and disc (I0I_{0}, hh, PAd, and qdq_{\rm d}) and the position of the galaxy centre (x0,y0)(x_{0},y_{0}). In GASP2D, each image pixel intensity is weighted according to the variance of its total observed photon counts due to the contribution of both galaxy and sky, and accounting for photon and detector read-out noise. Seeing effects were taken into account by convolving the model image with a circular Moffat point spread function (Moffat, 1969, hereafter PSF) with shape parameters measured from the stars in the galaxy image. Only the image pixels with an intensity larger than 1.5 times the sky standard deviation were included in the fit. Foreground stars were masked and excluded from the fit. The initial guesses were adopted to initialise the non-linear least-squares fit to galaxy image, where the parameters were all allowed to vary. A model of the galaxy surface brightness distribution was built using the fitted parameters. It was convolved with the adopted circular two-dimensional Moffat PSF and subtracted from the observed image to obtain a residual image. In order to confirm the minimum in the χ2\chi^{2}-space found in this first pass, two more iterations were performed. In these iterations, all the pixels and/or regions of the residual image with values greater or less than a fixed threshold, controlled by the user, were rejected. Those regions were masked out and the fit was repeated assuming, as initial trials for the free parameters, the values obtained in the previous iteration. These masks are useful when galaxies have spiral arms and dust lanes, which can affect the fitted parameters. We found that our algorithm converges after three iterations.

The model decompositions for few elliptical galaxies (NGC 4473, NGC 4636, NGC 4649) were significantly improved by including a disc component, as found in a few other elliptical galaxies (Kormendy et al., 2009; McDonald et al., 2009). For the other ellipticals, the values of rer_{\rm e} obtained either directly (empirically) from the light profile (in §3.1) or by using a Sérsic fitting function (from the two-dimensional photometric decomposition) agree within their respective errors.

We eliminated 33 galaxies from our sample because of poor decompositions due to either a strong central bar, a Freeman II profile (Freeman, 1970), or just the overall inadequacy of our single or double-component modelling (e.g., due to the presence of strong dust lanes and/or spiral arms). We successfully performed photometric decompositions, as judged by a global χ2\chi^{2} figure-of-merit, for the 57 galaxies ( 38 from Sample A, 19 from Sample B) listed in Table 4. The latter includes the resulting bulge and disc structural parameters. Some examples illustrating the various fitting strategies are shown in Figure 3. These are the same galaxies, whose azimuthally-averaged surface brightness profiles are shown in Figure 2. For all of them, the ellipse-averaged radial profiles of surface brightness, ellipticity, and position angle of the model image are consistent with those measured on the galaxy image. The differences between model and data found in the ellipticity and position angle of NGC 4477 and in the ellipticity of NGC 3675 are due to the presence of a weak bar and strong dust lanes, respectively. These features are clearly seen in the galaxies’ residual images. Nevertheless, the surface brightness residuals Δ​μi\Delta\mu_{i} are remarkably small; |Δ​μi|<0.2|\Delta\mu_{i}|<0.2 mag arcsec-2 for all the galaxies shown in Figure 3, except for some portions of the dust lanes of NGC 3675 where the residuals increase to ∼0.4\sim 0.4 mag arcsec-2. Although part of the NGC 3675 disc is missing, this does not affect the fit result. GASP2D performs a reliable fit as soon as the observed galaxy can be modelled by the sum of two axisymmetric components and the field of view covers at least half of the galaxy (Méndez-Abreu, 2008).

The GASP2D formal errors obtained from the χ2\chi^{2} minimisation method are not representative of the real errors in the structural parameters (Méndez-Abreu et al., 2008). Instead, the estimated errors given in Table 4 were obtained through a series of Monte Carlo simulations. To this end, we generated a set of 400 images of elliptical galaxies with a Sérsic spheroid and 400 images of disc galaxies with a Sérsic bulge and an exponential disc; each with a different PA and ellipticity. The range of tested parameters for the simulated images was taken from the photometric analysis of nearby elliptical galaxies by Kormendy et al. (2009) and face-on disc galaxies by Gadotti (2009) (but assuming a wider range of axial ratios than the latter). Our tests include treatment for resolution effects (galaxy distance, pixel scale, and seeing), colour effects (accounting for VV and ii bands), inclination, and more. The two-dimensional parametric decomposition was applied to analyse the images of the artificial galaxies as if they were real. The artificial and observed galaxies were divided in bins of 1 mag. The relative errors on the fitted parameters of the artificial galaxies were estimated by comparing the input and output values and were assumed to be normally distributed. In each magnitude bin, the mean and standard deviation of relative errors of artificial galaxies were adopted as the systematic and typical error on the relevant parameter for the observed galaxies. Overall, we find that GASP2D recovers the galaxy structural parameters with an uncertainty ranging from 1%, to 10%, and to 20% for brighter (6.5≤mtot,i<7.56.5\leq m_{{\rm tot},i}<7.5), intermediate (10.5≤mtot,i<11.510.5\leq m_{{\rm tot},i}<11.5), and fainter (12.5≤mtot,i<13.512.5\leq m_{{\rm tot},i}<13.5) sample galaxies, respectively.

The inclination of disc galaxies was calculated from the fitted disc axial ratio in the ii-band as

sin2⁡i=1−qd21−q02,\sin^{2}i=\frac{1-q_{\rm d}^{2}}{1-q_{0}^{2}}, (3)

where q0q_{0} is the intrinsic disc axial ratio. We obtain the latter from Paturel et al. (1997):

log⁡q0=−0.43−0.053​T,\log q_{0}=-0.43-0.053\;T, (4)

where TT is the galaxy Hubble type from RC3.

The fitted ii-band disc axial ratios agree well with the isophotal axial ratios at a surface brightness level μB=25\mu_{B}=25 mag arcsec-2 reported in the RC3. Our disc axial ratios are on average 6%6\% lower than RC3 with a standard deviation of 7%7\%. We adopted the RC3 axial ratios for the lenticular and spiral galaxies whose GASP2D solution for the disc was too uncertain; this amounts to 28 galaxies in Sample A and another 8 in Sample B.

3.3 Stellar Velocity Dispersion

The measured stellar velocity dispersions, σ\sigma, for galaxies in Sample A were taken from the same sources as 12. We applied the aperture correction of Jørgensen et al. (1995) to transform the σ\sigma into the equivalent of an effective stellar dispersions, σe\sigma_{\rm e}, measured within a circular aperture of radius re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge}. The effective radii were also taken from the same sources as 12, except for the 35 galaxies for which re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} was obtained from our own decomposition of the SDSS images (Tables 3 and 4). The maximum difference between our and literature values of re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} is about 20%20\%, though the comparison often involves different band passes which broadens the discrepancy.

The aperture correction was also applied to the σ\sigma measured for NGC 2892 and NGC 5921 by Ho et al. (2009) and Wegner et al. (2003), respectively.

For Sample B galaxies, we adopted the values of σe\sigma_{\rm e} given by 66. These were derived as the luminosity-weighted mean of the stellar velocity dispersion within re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge}.

3.4 Circular Velocity

The values for the galaxy circular velocity, VcV_{\rm c}, for both elliptical and disc galaxies were collected from different sources.

We retrieved VcV_{\rm c} from the compilation of Ho (2007) for 40 disc galaxies (31 from Sample A, 9 from Sample B). These were derived from the H i line widths available in the HyperLeda catalogue (Paturel et al., 2003). The W20W_{20} and W50W_{50} line widths are measured at 20%20\% and the 50%50\% of the total H i line profile flux. For galaxies missing in Ho (2007), line widths were found in HyperLeda for an additional 27 galaxies (22 from the Sample A, 5 from Sample B). Given multiple sources in HyperLeda, we favoured the larger survey source for each galaxy in order maximise the homogeneity of the data base33 3 We selected the most recent and highest resolution observations available in the on-line HyperLeda catalogue (http://leda.univ-lyon1.fr) up to September 2009.. All line widths were already corrected for instrumental resolution. We further applied a correction for cosmological stretching and broadening by gas turbulence following Bottinelli et al. (1983) and Verheijen & Sancisi (2001). Finally, the corrected line widths W20,corrW_{\rm 20,corr} and W50,corrW_{\rm 50,corr} were deprojected using the prescription of Paturel et al. (1997)

V20\displaystyle V_{20} =\displaystyle= 0.5​(101.187​log⁡W20,corr−0.543)/sin⁡i,\displaystyle 0.5(10^{1.187\log W_{\rm 20,corr}-0.543})/\sin i, (5)
V50\displaystyle V_{50} =\displaystyle= 0.5​(101.071​log⁡W50,corr−0.210)/sin⁡i,\displaystyle 0.5(10^{1.071\log W_{\rm 50,corr}-0.210})/\sin i, (6)

where the inclination, ii, is listed in Table 1 and 2. We take the final circular velocity as the average of V20V_{20} and V50V_{50},

Vc=(V20+V50)/2.V_{\rm c}=(V_{20}+V_{50})/2. (7)

Following Ho (2007), we adopted a 5% error on VcV_{\rm c} for the maximum velocity listed in Hyperleda.

For 14 early-type galaxies (7 in Sample A, 7 in Sample B), we adopted the value of VcV_{\rm c} derived from dynamical modelling (IC 1459, Samurović & Danziger 2005; NGC 1052, Binney et al. 1990; NGC 3115, Bender et al. 1994; NGC 3608, Coccato et al. 2009; NGC 4314 Quillen et al. 1994; and 9 ellipticals in Kronawitter et al. 2000). For a few other galaxies (five in Sample A, one in Sample B), either the ionised-gas (NGC 2911, Sil’chenko & Afanasiev 2004; NGC 5252, Morse et al. 1998), the H i (IC 342, Pizzella et al. 2005; NGC 3801, Hota et al. 2009) or the CO kinematics (NGC 4526, Young et al. 2008), Milky Way (Baes et al. 2003) rotational velocity at large radii are assumed to represent VcV_{\rm c}. We adopted a 10% error when the VcV_{\rm c} uncertainty from models or observations was not given.

Finally, we eliminated 7 galaxies (4 from Sample A, 3 from Sample B) since their quoted circular velocities are unrealistically low (NGC 1497, NGC 3384, and NGC 5576, Paturel et al. 2003; NGC 3642, NGC 4429, NGC 5347, and NGC 7052, Ho 2007).

The final circular velocities of 88 galaxies from Sample A (65) and Sample B (23) are listed in Tables 1 and 2.

3.5 Masses

We estimated the bulge mass as MbulgeM_{\rm bulge}=α​re,bulge​σe2/G=\alpha\;r_{\rm e,bulge}\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}/G, where GG is the gravitational constant and α=5.0±0.1\alpha=5.0\pm 0.1 (Cappellari et al., 2006) is a dimensionless constant that depends on galaxy structure. The effective radius, re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge}, for elliptical galaxies is extracted from their azimuthally-averaged light profile (Table 3), whereas the bulge effective radius of lenticular and spiral galaxies is obtained from two-dimensional photometric decomposition (Table 4). In deriving MbulgeM_{\rm bulge}, we implicitly assumed that the measured value of σe\sigma_{\rm e} is dominated by the bulge component. For late-type galaxies we expect that the disc contribution to σe\sigma_{\rm e} results in an increase of the scatter of MbulgeM_{\rm bulge} as a function of the morphological type. This does not affect our analysis since we could measure re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} (and therefore MbulgeM_{\rm bulge}) for only a few Sb–Sbc galaxies. Moreover, the ratio B/T>0.1B/T>0.1 except for three galaxies.

Ferrarese et al. (2006) suggested a connection between M∙M_{\bullet} and the mass of early-type galaxies calculated as

Me,gal=α​re,gal​σe2/G​with​α=5.0±0.1.M_{\rm e,gal}\,=\,\alpha\,\ r_{\rm e,gal}\sigma_{\rm e}^{2}/G\ {\rm with}\ \alpha=5.0\pm 0.1. (8)

Note that such a mass estimate is indicative of the galaxy mass within re,galr_{\rm e,gal} and is thus an incomplete representation of the total galaxy mass. We calculated Me,galM_{\rm e,gal} for the elliptical and lenticular galaxies in our sample by adopting re,galr_{\rm e,gal} calculated from the azimuthally-averaged light profiles (Table 3). For elliptical galaxies, MbulgeM_{\rm bulge}=\,=\,Me,galM_{\rm e,gal}. The virial estimator by Cappellari et al. (2006) captures the entire dynamical mass so long as total mass traces light (Thomas et al., 2011). Wolf et al. (2010) found a different coefficient (α=4\alpha=4) for their derivation of a mass estimator for stellar systems supported by velocity dispersion. The latter is a good estimate of the total dynamical mass inside a radius which is just larger than the effective radius (Thomas et al., 2011). The appropriate value of α\alpha is actually a function of the Sérsic shape index nn (Trujillo et al., 2004; Cappellari et al., 2006). However the exact application of the α⁡(n)\alpha(n) relation, which results in a zero-point offset for Me,galM_{\rm e,gal}, does not affect our conclusions. We thus make use of the Cappellari et al. (2006) mass estimator. Error estimates on MbulgeM_{\rm bulge} and Me,galM_{\rm e,gal} account for the uncertainty on α\alpha.

We derived the dynamical mass of the disc galaxies from

Mdyn=R​Vc2/G,M_{\rm dyn}\,=\,R\,V_{\rm c}^{2}/G, (9)

where R=r24.5R=r_{24.5} (Table 3). Most of the circular velocities that we derived from H i data yield no information about their radial coverage. Nevertheless, Mdyn,galM_{\rm dyn,gal} corresponds to the galaxy mass within the optical radius, because r24.5r_{24.5} is roughly indicative of the galaxy optical radius and the observations of spatially-resolved H i kinematics in spirals show that the size of H i discs closely matches that of a galaxy’s optical disc (Ho et al., 2008a).

The masses computed from Eq. (8) and Eq. (9) are both available only for the 10 lenticular galaxies in our sample, since they share dynamical properties of both elliptical and spiral galaxies. For these galaxies, ⟨\langleMdyn,galM_{\rm dyn,gal}/Me,galM_{\rm e,gal}⟩=1.27±1.07\rangle=1.27\pm 1.07.

The galaxy stellar masses, M⋆,galM_{\star,\rm gal}, were derived from Li,galL_{i,{\rm gal}} under the assumption of constant mass-to-light ratio (M/L)i(M/L)_{i}. (M/L)i(M/L)_{i} estimates were inferred from our g−ig-i colours following Bell et al. (2003). Their mass-to-light ratios were derived from the stellar population models of Bruzual & Charlot (2003), which are tuned to reproduce the ages and metallicities of the local spiral galaxies.

4 Analysis

4.1 Correlations Between M∙M_{\bullet} and Bulge and Galaxy Parameters

We used the data obtained in §3 to build scaling relations between M∙M_{\bullet} and the bulge (i.e., the velocity dispersion, luminosity, virial mass, Sérsic index, and mean effective surface brightness) and galaxy (luminosity, circular velocity, stellar, virial, and dynamical mass) properties. In addition to the Sample A++B, we also built a comparison sample with the 30 galaxies for which all the desired physical parameters could be measured. For each of the above parameters xx, we assume that there exists a relation of the form

log⁡M∙M⊙=α+β​log⁡xx0\log\frac{M_{\bullet}}{{\rm M}_{\odot}}\,=\,\alpha\,+\,\beta\,\log{\frac{x}{x_{0}}} (10)

where x0x_{0} is a normalisation value chosen near the mean of the distribution of x−x-values.

The best-fit values of α\alpha and β\beta, their associated uncertainties, the total scatter ϵ\epsilon and intrinsic scatter ϵintr\epsilon_{\rm intr} of the relation, the Spearman rank correlation coefficient ρ\rho, and the level of significance of the correlation PP were obtained as a function of the sample at hand. The results are given in Table 5. The quoted errors are all derived through a bootstrap technique.

Samples A++B and the comparison sample include both accurate determinations and upper limits of M∙M_{\bullet}. The proper handling of these heterogeneous data sets requires that we perform a censored regression analysis (Feigelson & Nelson, 1985; Isobe et al., 1986) with the ASURV44 4 The FORTRAN source code of the Astronomy Survival Analysis Package (v.1.3) is available at http://www2.astro.psu.edu/statcodes/asurv. package (Lavalley et al., 1992). Linear regressions were calculated with the EM maximum-likelihood algorithm implementing the technique of expectation (E-step) and maximization (M-step) by Dempster et al. (1977) which assumes normal residuals. For each relation, we checked that the distribution of residuals about the fitted line was normal. With uncensored data, this analysis would be equivalent to that of a standard least-squares linear regression. ASURV gives as correlation coefficient the generalised Spearman rank correlation coefficient ρ\rho (Akritas, 1989) and computes the level of significance of the correlation PP. We derived the scatter of the relation ϵ\epsilon as the root-mean square (rms) deviation in log⁡(M∙/M⊙)\log(M_{\bullet}/{\rm M}_{\odot}) from the fitted relation assuming no measurement errors. This assumption does not affect our results, since we wish to compare the relative tightness of the different scaling relations for the comparison sample.

66 focused their analysis on M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} and M∙−Li,bulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{i,{\rm bulge}}. We have extended their analysis to a broader range of scaling relations by performing least-square linear regressions with the secure values of M∙M_{\bullet} and the bulge and galaxy parameters measured for Sample B. We used the MPFITEXY55 5 The IDL source code of MPFITEXY is available at http://purl.org/mike/mpfitexy/. algorithm (Williams et al., 2010), which accounts for measurement errors in both variables and the intrinsic scatter ϵintr\epsilon_{\rm intr} of the relation. We used the IDL routine R_CORRELATE to compute the standard Spearman rank correlation coefficient ρ\rho and the level of significance of the correlation. The intrinsic scatter of each relation was assessed by varying ϵintr\epsilon_{\rm intr} in the fitting process to ensure that the reduced χν2=1\chi_{\nu}^{2}=1. The total scatter ϵ\epsilon was derived as the rms deviation in log⁡(M∙/M⊙)\log(M_{\bullet}/{\rm M}_{\odot}) from the fitted relation weighted by measurement errors.

In addition to fitting the M∙M_{\bullet}–bulge and galaxy scaling relations as outlined above, we also look in the subsections below for correlations against morphological type or nuclear activity as listed in Tables 1 and 2. We will see that the latter (morphology or nuclear activity) do not play a strong rôle in any of the M∙M_{\bullet}–bulge and galaxy scaling relations. Morphology only plays a small rôle in the M∙−M⋆,galM_{\bullet}-M_{\star,\rm gal} and in the M∙−VcM_{\bullet}-V_{\rm c} relations.

4.1.1 M∙M_{\bullet} versus σe\sigma_{\rm e}

We have plotted the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} distribution for the Sample A++B in Figure 4. The slope of our M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation is consistent within the errors with those by Ferrarese & Ford (2005) and Lauer et al. (2007) as discussed by 12, and with that by 66 by default. On the other hand, the inclusion of the upper limits measured by 12 and 66 slightly changes the zero point of the relation but does not appreciably affect its scatter. The M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation is indeed the tightest correlation that we measure; its scatter is consistent with 66 (ϵ=0.44±0.06\epsilon=0.44\pm 0.06 dex) and slightly larger than Ferrarese & Ford (2005, = ϵ 0.34 dex). According to 66, the increased fraction of spirals may be a source of the increased scatter with respect to previous estimates based mostly on SMBH measurements in early-type galaxies. Consistently, our analysis reveals that the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} scatter for late-type galaxies (ϵ=0.52±0.14\epsilon=0.52\pm 0.14 dex) alone is slightly larger than that of early-type galaxies (ϵ=0.38±0.04\epsilon=0.38\pm 0.04 dex). Nevertheless, at small σe\sigma_{\rm e}, some upper limits exceed the expected M∙M_{\bullet} as the line-widths for such low-σe\sigma_{\rm e} outliers are most likely affected by the mass contribution of a conspicuous nuclear cluster (12). The scatter for the late-type galaxies reduces to (ϵ=0.38±0.05\epsilon=0.38\pm 0.05 dex) by excluding the nucleated galaxies from the fit. Therefore, they are the cause for the observed difference between the scatter of early and late-type galaxies. We conclude that the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation is the same for both early and late-type galaxies. S0 galaxies overlap ellipticals at high σe\sigma_{\rm e} values and spirals at low σe\sigma_{\rm e} values.

Barred and unbarred galaxies follow the same M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation within the errors. The same is not true for galaxies with classical and pseudo-bulge. We have classified our bulges according to their measured Sérsic index (Kormendy & Kennicutt, 2004, n>2n>2 for classical and n≤2n\leq 2 for pseudo-bulges;). We find slope differences in the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relations of our 46 classical (β=3.86±0.71\beta=3.86\pm 0.71) and 11 pseudo-bulges (β=5.63±0.86\beta=5.63\pm 0.86), whereas their zero points (α=8.09±0.09\alpha=8.09\pm 0.09 and α=7.78±0.33\alpha=7.78\pm 0.33, respectively) are in closer agreement within the errors. Conversely, Hu (2008) found similar slopes and different zero points. At face values, our and Hu et al.’s correlation coefficients are in agreement. This is mostly due to the large error bars on the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} coefficients for pseudo-bulges, which translate into a lower level of significance of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation for pseudo-bulges (P<2%P<2\%) with respect to that for classical bulges (P<0.1%P<0.1\%). This results supports the recent findings by Kormendy et al. (2011) that there is little or no correlation between M∙M_{\bullet} and pseudo-bulges.

At high σe\sigma_{\rm e} values, the M∙M_{\bullet} of the Sample A++B shows a weak steepening with respect to M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} confirming previous results by Wyithe (2006), Lauer et al. (2007), and Dalla Bontà et al. (2009).

Finally, Figure 4 shows the absence of trends of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation with nuclear activity. The different types of nuclear activity cover all the σe\sigma_{\rm e} range, with most LINERs at high σe\sigma_{\rm e} and most Seyferts at low σe\sigma_{\rm e}. This is expected considering the strong dependence of nuclear spectral class on Hubble type (and therefore on σe\sigma_{\rm e}), with LINERs and Seyfert nuclei being more frequent in ellipticals and spirals, respectively (see Ho, 2008, for a review).

4.1.2 M∙M_{\bullet} versus Li,bulgeL_{i,{\rm bulge}}

The correlation between M∙M_{\bullet} and the luminosity of the spheroidal component of a galaxy is also fairly tight (see Graham 2007, and references therein). Graham (2007) compared the different versions of the M∙−LbulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm bulge} by Kormendy & Gebhardt (2001), McLure & Dunlop (2002), Marconi & Hunt (2003), and Erwin et al. (2004). Recently, Sani et al. (2011) derived the M∙−LbulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm bulge} relation by measuring the 3.6 μ\mum bulge luminosity. Since the differing relations do not predict the same SMBH mass, Graham (2007) investigated the effects of possible biases on the M∙−LbulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm bulge} relation including any dependency on the Hubble constant, the correction for dust attenuation in the bulges of disc galaxies, the mis-classification of lenticular galaxies as elliptical galaxies and the adopted regression analysis. These adjustments resulted in relations which are consistent with each other and suitable for predicting similar M∙M_{\bullet}. In particular, a detailed photometric decomposition of the galaxy light profile is crucial to obtaining a representative bulge luminosity and therefore a reliable M∙−LbulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm bulge}.

66 derived an updated value of the intrinsic scatter of the M∙−LbulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm bulge} relation, which is comparable to that of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation in early-type galaxies, confirming the results of Marconi & Hunt (2003). According to them, the scatter of the M∙−LbulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm bulge} relation is significantly reduced when the bulge effective radius is extracted from a careful two-dimensional image decomposition.

Figure 5 shows our M∙−Li,bulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{i,{\rm bulge}} relation. The best-fit coefficients are in agreement within the errors with Graham (2007) and Sani et al. (2011). The scatter is slightly higher than 66 who fit only early-type galaxies, but larger than that of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation. All galaxies show a similar M∙−Li,bulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{i,{\rm bulge}} distribution with no dependence on morphological type or nuclear activity. We cannot test the claim that barred and unbarred galaxies follow different M∙−Li,bulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{i,{\rm bulge}} relations (Graham, 2008; Graham & Li, 2009; Gadotti & Kauffmann, 2009; Hu, 2009), since the sample galaxies with a strong bar were excluded for photometric decomposition and thus lack a Li,bulgeL_{i,{\rm bulge}} measurement. For all the remaining galaxies, we did not model any other components than the bulge and disc (see Table 4).

4.1.3 M∙M_{\bullet} versus MbulgeM_{\rm bulge}

The connection between the M∙M_{\bullet} and LbulgeL_{\rm bulge} suggests a linear correlation with mass of the spheroidal component of the galaxy (Magorrian et al., 1998; McLure & Dunlop, 2002; Marconi & Hunt, 2003; Häring & Rix, 2004).

The slope of our M∙−MbulgeM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm bulge} relation (Fig. 6) is consistent within the errors with McLure & Dunlop (2002), Marconi & Hunt (2003), Aller & Richstone (2007) and Sani et al. (2011) and slightly shallower than Häring & Rix (2004). This regression is not a marked improvement over the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation, as one might expect considering the additional fitting parameter in the mass measurement (namely the radius). Indeed, the M∙−MbulgeM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm bulge} is worse than the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation. However, MbulgeM_{\rm bulge} is still a better proxy for M∙M_{\bullet} than Li,bulgeL_{i,{\rm bulge}}. Different Hubble types follow the same M∙−MbulgeM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm bulge} relation, with the lenticular galaxies covering the whole range of masses. There is also no dependence of this relation on nuclear activity, in agreement with McLure & Dunlop (2002).

4.1.4 M∙M_{\bullet} versus Sérsic n and ⟨μe,bulge⟩\langle\mu_{\rm e,bulge}\rangle

The two-dimensional photometric decompositions yield a panoply of galaxy structural parameters, including the Sérsic shape index nn and mean effective surface brightness ⟨μe,bulge⟩\langle\mu_{\rm e,bulge}\rangle, both used as measure of the concentration of the bulge light. The Sérsic index nn has indeed been adopted by some as a good tracer for M∙M_{\bullet} (Graham et al., 2001; Graham et al., 2003; Graham & Driver, 2007).

Our M∙M_{\bullet}−-nn relation (Figure 7) differs significantly from the linear and quadratic relations with log\log M∙M_{\bullet} and log\log nn by Graham et al. (2001); Graham et al. (2003) and Graham & Driver (2007), respectively. In particular, the values of nn for galaxies with high M∙M_{\bullet} are not as large as those in Graham & Driver (2007). The relation is characterised by a large scatter, small Spearman correlation coefficient, and low level of significance. Therefore, the correlation between M∙M_{\bullet} and nn is poor and the M∙M_{\bullet}−-nn relation is not reliable for predicting M∙M_{\bullet}. Our findings are in agreement with Hopkins et al. (2007b) who found no correlation between M∙M_{\bullet} and Sérsic index with both observations and hydrodynamical simulations.

The correlation between M∙M_{\bullet} and ⟨μe,bulge⟩\langle\mu_{\rm e,bulge}\rangle (Figure 8) is also poor, lending further support to the idea that M∙M_{\bullet} is unrelated to the light concentration of the bulge, regardless of galaxy morphology and nuclear activity.

4.1.5 M∙M_{\bullet} versus Li,galL_{i,{\rm gal}}

Kormendy (2001) compared the BB-band total magnitude with dynamically secure M∙M_{\bullet} estimates in spheroids and few bulgeless disc galaxies. The poor correlation between M∙M_{\bullet} and Li,galL_{i,{\rm gal}} led him to conclude that the evolution of SMBHs is linked to bulges rather than discs.

We compared our own Li,galL_{i,{\rm gal}} with M∙M_{\bullet} as a function of the morphological type in Figure 9. The Spearman rank correlation coefficient suggests a correlation at 17% significance level, which is tighter than Kormendy (2001) but not as tight as that for the M∙−LbulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm bulge} relation. Our sample is short of bulgeless galaxies which may explain the better agreement for our M∙M_{\bullet} and Li,galL_{i,{\rm gal}} with respect to Kormendy (2001). On the other hand, total and bulge luminosity differ for disc galaxies. The later the morphological type, the larger the discrepancy resulting in both a larger slope and scatter of the M∙−Li,galM_{\bullet}-L_{i,{\rm gal}} relation with respect to M∙−LbulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm bulge}. The scatter is larger and the correlation weaker when the g−g-band total luminosity is considered. Our findings are consistent with Hu (2009, see their Fig. 6) and confirm that bulge luminosity is a better tracer of the mass of SMBHs than total light of the galaxy.

4.1.6 M∙M_{\bullet} versus M⋆,galM_{\star,\rm gal}, Me,galM_{\rm e,gal}, and Mdyn,galM_{\rm dyn,gal}

We have tested whether the scatter in predicting M∙M_{\bullet} could be reduced by adopting M⋆,galM_{\star,\rm gal} rather than Li,galL_{i,{\rm gal}}, since the galaxy luminosity is a proxy for its stellar mass. The M∙−M⋆,galM_{\bullet}-M_{\star,\rm gal} relation shown in Figure 10 is a slight improvement over the M∙−Li,galM_{\bullet}-L_{i,{\rm gal}} relation. The slopes are comparable but the Spearman rank correlation coefficient of the former is higher with a 3% significance level. Ellipticals and lenticulars follow a tighter M∙−M⋆,galM_{\bullet}-M_{\star,\rm gal} relation than late-type galaxies; the disc light clearly plays an anti-correlating rôle, indicating once more that the bulge parameters drive SMBH correlations.

We adopted the mass estimator from Cappellari et al. (2006) (i.e., the mass within the effective radius) for our ellipticals and lenticulars. The distribution of M∙M_{\bullet} as a function of Me,galM_{\rm e,gal} for the early-type galaxies is plotted in Figure 11. They follow the same trend as the M∙−Me,galM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm e,gal} relation by Ferrarese et al. (2006). This is especially true for Me,galM_{\rm e,gal}>1011>10^{11} M⊙ where the fit slope and normalisation are consistent within the errors with Ferrarese et al. (2006). Less-massive galaxies seem to follow a steeper M∙−Me,galM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm e,gal} relation with a smaller normalisation. More data are however needed in this mass range to carefully address any trend differences. Introducing a new parameter re,galr_{\rm e,gal} and a specific exponent for σe\sigma_{\rm e} ought to considerably reduce the scatter of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation but, in fact, it does not. In particular, the scatter of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation is smaller than that of M∙−Me,galM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm e,gal} if the same sample of early-type galaxies is considered.

The dynamical mass Mdyn,galM_{\rm dyn,gal} (i.e., the mass within the optical radius) was taken as the galaxy mass estimator for lenticulars and spirals. It does not correlate with M∙M_{\bullet} (Figure 12), irrespective of Hubble type and nuclear activity. Our analysis reveals that the coarse M∙M_{\bullet}−-Mdyn,galM_{\rm dyn,gal} relation found by Ho et al. (2008b, = ϵ 0.61 dex) does not hold when galaxies with Mdyn,galM_{\rm dyn,gal}≤1010\leq 10^{10} M⊙ (i.e., at the lower mass end of the Mdyn,galM_{\rm dyn,gal} range) are taken into account. The scatter of the M∙M_{\bullet}–galaxy mass relation is larger and the correlation weaker when M⋆,galM_{\star,\rm gal} and Mdyn,galM_{\rm dyn,gal} are considered. Since the stellar and dynamical masses include the mass contribution of the disc component, we conclude that the bulge mass is a better tracer of M∙M_{\bullet}. Nevertheless, the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} is tighter and yet again more fundamental than the M∙−Me,galM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm e,gal} relation.

4.1.7 M∙−VcM_{\bullet}-V_{\rm c} and Vc−σeV_{\rm c}-\sigma_{\rm e} relations

Assuming that VcV_{\rm c} at large radii trace the dark matter halo, we study the possible link between SMBHs and dark matter halos by comparing M∙M_{\bullet} with VcV_{\rm c}. A possible relation between M∙M_{\bullet} and the dark matter depends clearly on the radius at which VcV_{\rm c} is measured. Theoretical models that reproduce the observed luminosity function of quasars (Cattaneo, 2001; Adams et al., 2003; Volonteri et al., 2003; Hopkins et al., 2005a; Springel et al., 2005) suggest that M∙M_{\bullet} scales as a power law of the virial velocity (i.e., the circular velocity of the galactic halo at the virial radius) of the galactic halo of the SMBH host. However, the conversion between VcV_{\rm c} measured at large radii and virial velocity, depends on the assumed model.

We show M∙M_{\bullet} against VcV_{\rm c} in Figure 13. There is a weak correlation between these quantities, which is mostly driven by the late-type galaxies.

This is in agreement with previous studies by Zasov et al. (2005) and Ho et al. (2008b). Zasov et al. (2005) used a collection of 41 galaxies with M∙M_{\bullet}, σe\sigma_{\rm e}, and VcV_{\rm c} from the literature to conclude that there is a coarse M∙M_{\bullet}−-VcV_{\rm c} relation and that, for a given VcV_{\rm c}, early-type galaxies have larger M∙M_{\bullet} than late-type galaxies. Ho et al. (2008b) studied the M∙−VcM_{\bullet}-V_{\rm c} relation for a sample of 154 nearby galaxies comprising both early and late-type systems for which M∙M_{\bullet} was estimated from the mass-luminosity-line width relation (Kaspi et al., 2000; Greene & Ho, 2005; Peterson & Bentz, 2006) and VcV_{\rm c} from H i and optical data (Ho et al., 2008a). They found that the correlation between M∙M_{\bullet} and VcV_{\rm c} improves if only the galaxies with the most reliable VcV_{\rm c} measurements are considered. The distribution of our spiral galaxies is consistent with the M∙M_{\bullet}−-VcV_{\rm c} relation by Ho et al. (2008b), whereas the value of M∙M_{\bullet} for elliptical and lenticular galaxies is almost constant over the full observed VcV_{\rm c} range (Figure 13).

Ho et al. (2008b) suggested that the main source of scatter in the M∙M_{\bullet}−-VcV_{\rm c} relation is related to the dependence of VcV_{\rm c}/σe\sigma_{\rm e} on the bulge-to-disc ratio (Courteau et al., 2007; Ho, 2007). Since the bulge-to-disc ratio scales with the light concentration (Doi et al., 1993), which is another way to estimate the degree of bulge dominance, we derived VcV_{\rm c}/σe\sigma_{\rm e} as a function of C28C_{28}. We found a general agreement with the relation found by Courteau et al. (2007). The Jeans equation evokes a relation between the circular velocity of galaxy and its velocity dispersion for a pressure-supported system. The VcV_{\rm c}/σe\sigma_{\rm e} relation was first reported by Whitmore et al. (1979) and more recently by Ferrarese (2002), Buyle et al. (2004), and Pizzella et al. (2005). Courteau et al. (2007) and Ho (2007) further demonstrated that the VcV_{\rm c}−-σe\sigma_{\rm e} relation must depend on a third parameter which depends on the galaxy structure.

The existence of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation and the absence of a single universal Vc−σeV_{\rm c}-\sigma_{\rm e} for all the morphological types is in contrast with the hypothesis that M∙M_{\bullet} is more fundamentally connected to halo than to bulge, as suggested by Ferrarese (2002) and Pizzella et al. (2005). We conclude that the SMBH mass is associated with the bulge and not the halo (Peng, 2010, see also) by analysing the Vc−σeV_{\rm c}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation as a function of M∙M_{\bullet} for our sample galaxies (Figure 14). For a given M∙M_{\bullet}, the range of VcV_{\rm c} is on average 1.6 times larger than the range of σe\sigma_{\rm e} demonstrating that M∙M_{\bullet} is driven by σe\sigma_{\rm e} and not by VcV_{\rm c}. The few bulgeless galaxies known to host a SMBH (NGC 4395, Filippenko & Ho 2003; POX 52, Barth et al. 2004; NGC 1042, Shields et al. 2008) are an exception to this scenario, which is supported by cases like M33. The latter is a pure disc galaxy, which does not show any evidence of a SMBH (Gebhardt et al., 2001) but has a massive dark matter halo (Corbelli, 2003).

More recently, Kormendy & Bender (2011) confirmed our early findings (Beifiori, 2010) by extending the analysis of the VcV_{\rm c}−-σe\sigma_{\rm e} relation to bulgeless galaxies. They reported an absence of correlation between VcV_{\rm c} and σe\sigma_{\rm e} unless the galaxy also contains a bulge, suggesting that the fundamental driver for M∙M_{\bullet} is σe\sigma_{\rm e} for all Hubble types and that VcV_{\rm c} plays only a small rôle in galaxies with a bulge. Although at this later cosmic time the M∙M_{\bullet}−-VcV_{\rm c} is coarser than the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation, Volonteri et al. (2011) remind us that a tighter connection in the past is not precluded. At earlier epochs, the SMBH assembly was more likely coupled to the dark matter halo properties based on a merger-driven hierarchical formation scenario. Still, the scatter we measure for the M∙M_{\bullet}−-VcV_{\rm c} relation is a factor ∼2\sim 2 larger than that of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation, which is significantly more than argued by Volonteri et al. (2011) in their analysis of Kormendy & Bender (2011)’s data set.

4.2 Correlations Between M∙M_{\bullet} and Linear Combinations of Bulge and Galaxy Parameters

We wish to understand whether the relations between M∙M_{\bullet} and bulge and galaxy properties studied in §4.1 can be improved by the addition of a third parameter. For the bulge or the galaxy parameters xx and yy in Table 6, a correlation of the form

log⁡M∙M⊙=γ+α​log⁡xx0+β​log⁡yy0\log\frac{M_{\bullet}}{{\rm M}_{\odot}}\,=\,\gamma\,+\,\alpha\,\log{\frac{x}{x_{0}}}+\,\beta\,\log{\frac{y}{y_{0}}} (11)

is assumed, where x0x_{0} and y0y_{0} are normalisation values chosen near the mean of the distribution of xx and yy values respectively. The fit parameters are the offset γ\gamma, and the logarithmic slopes α\alpha and β\beta. The best-fit values of α\alpha, β\beta, and γ\gamma, their associated uncertainties, the total scatter ϵ\epsilon and intrinsic scatter ϵintr\epsilon_{\rm intr} of the relation are given in Table 6. The Spearman rank test cannot be evaluated in the same way as described in §4.1 as it applies to two variables. To estimate the degree of correlations between the parameters in use, we applied the Spearman rank statistic using the projections of the planes once the combination of the two independent variables has been fixed to its best-fit values. This provides an indication of the degree of correlation between several linear combinations. The Spearman rank correlation coefficient ρ\rho, and the significance of the correlation PP derived for the projections are also given in Table 6. The quoted errors are all computed through a bootstrap technique.

For both Samples A++B and the comparison sample, we performed a censored regression analysis with two independent variables assuming normal residuals. The best-fit parameters were computed with the EM algorithm implemented in the ASURV package which yields maximum likelihood estimates from a censored data set allowing, in the general form, N observables distributed via a multivariate Gaussian distribution. We applied this technique to the special case of two independent variables and another dependent variable containing the censored data. The regression problem solves like a least-square fit but accounting for censored data. It uses initial guesses from an ordinary linear regression of the non-censored data and then converges on the new censored values.

The standard deviation is estimated in the standard fashion, weighted for a factor which accounts for the censored data (see Isobe et al., 1986, for details). The generalised Spearman rank correlation coefficient, and the significance of the correlation for the projections of planes, are based on the technique described in Akritas (1989). The total scatter was computed as the rms deviation in log⁡(M∙/M⊙)\log(M_{\bullet}/{\rm M}_{\odot}) from the fitted relation assuming no measurement errors.

We used our own modified version of the MPFITEXY algorithm to perform a least-squares linear regression of Sample B’s data with two independent variables. Measurement errors were invoked in the derivation of best-fit parameters, total, and intrinsic scatter. The Spearman rank correlation coefficient and level of significance of the correlation were also derived by using the projections of the best-fit plane given all possible parameter combinations. The actual computation was done using the IDL routine R_CORRELATE.

4.2.1 M∙M_{\bullet} versus Bulge Parameters

So far we have found that M∙M_{\bullet} is more strongly related with σe\sigma_{\rm e} than Li,bulgeL_{i,{\rm bulge}} and MbulgeM_{\rm bulge}. Nevertheless, the correlation between the M∙M_{\bullet} and MbulgeM_{\rm bulge} suggests that a possible combination of the bulge properties can result in a tighter correlation with M∙M_{\bullet}. Note that the BHFP derives from the FP which connects re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge}, σe\sigma_{\rm e}, and ⟨μe,bulge⟩\langle\mu_{\rm e,bulge}\rangle together (Dressler et al., 1987; Djorgovski & Davis, 1987; Jørgensen et al., 2007, and reference therein). Therefore, we have analysed the residuals of M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e}, M∙−LbulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm bulge}, and M∙−MbulgeM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm bulge} relations to test whether there is the evidence for an additional dependence with an additional parameter. The residuals were obtained as the difference between the observed data and their expected values from the fitting relations in Table 5. We compared the residuals in log⁡(M∙/M∙​[σe])\log(M_{\bullet}/M_{\bullet}[\sigma_{\rm e}]), log⁡(M∙/M∙​[Li,bulge])\log(M_{\bullet}/M_{\bullet}[L_{i,{\rm bulge}}]), and log⁡(M∙/M∙​[Mbulge])\log(M_{\bullet}/M_{\bullet}[\rm M_{bulge}]) with the bulge photometric and kinematic properties (i.e., ⟨μe,bulge⟩\langle\mu_{\rm e,bulge}\rangle, re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge}, nn, and σe\sigma_{\rm e}; Figure 15). There is no trend between log⁡(M∙/M∙​[σe])\log(M_{\bullet}/M_{\bullet}[\sigma_{\rm e}]) and other bulge properties (Figure 15, left column), whereas log⁡(M∙/M∙​[Li,bulge])\log(M_{\bullet}/M_{\bullet}[L_{i,{\rm bulge}}]) and log⁡(M∙/M∙​[Mbulge])\log(M_{\bullet}/M_{\bullet}[\rm M_{bulge}]) show a very weak dependence on re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} according to the the Spearman rank correlation coefficient and their significance intervals ∼6\sim 6% and ∼2\sim 2%, respectively (Figure 15, middle and left columns, respectively). This was confirmed by Sani et al. (2011), who found no correlation of the residual with rer_{\rm e}.

We have tested for the more fundamental driver of M∙M_{\bullet}. To this aim we considered different linear combinations of the bulge parameters with M∙M_{\bullet} (Figure 16). The correlation between M∙M_{\bullet}, σe\sigma_{\rm e}, and re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} is as tight as the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} (Figure 16a). Taking into account re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} does not significantly improve the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} fit. The relation between M∙M_{\bullet}, Li,bulgeL_{i,{\rm bulge}}, and re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} (Figure 16b) is not as strong as that between M∙M_{\bullet}, σe\sigma_{\rm e}, and re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge}, but it is a slight improvement over M∙−Li,bulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{i,{\rm bulge}}. The relation between M∙M_{\bullet}, σe\sigma_{\rm e}, and Li,bulgeL_{i,{\rm bulge}} is as tight as that between M∙M_{\bullet}, σe\sigma_{\rm e}, and re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} (Figure 16c). The relation between M∙M_{\bullet}, σe\sigma_{\rm e}, and MbulgeM_{\rm bulge} (Figure 16d) is expected since MbulgeM_{\rm bulge} is known to correlate with M∙M_{\bullet} and it depends on both σe\sigma_{\rm e} and re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge}. For this reason the two correlations with M∙M_{\bullet} and either σe\sigma_{\rm e} and MbulgeM_{\rm bulge} or re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} and MbulgeM_{\rm bulge} are different (but not independent) expressions of the same relationship. Thus, larger SMBHs are associated with more massive and larger bulges, as understood in the framework of coevolution of spheroids and SMBHs. Hopkins et al. (2007a); Hopkins et al. (2007b) first studied the residuals of the M∙−MbulgeM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm bulge} and M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relations with bulge properties, finding tighter correlations between the combination of the bulge parameters and M∙M_{\bullet}. This bolstered the notion of a BHFP. The bulge parameters MbulgeM_{\rm bulge} and Li,bulgeL_{i,{\rm bulge}} are indeed physically related to each other through the fundamental plane relation (FP) and virial theorem. The existence of such BHFP has important implications for the largest M∙M_{\bullet} and resolves the apparent conflict between expected and measured values of M∙M_{\bullet} for the outliers in both M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} and M∙−MbulgeM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm bulge} relations (Bernardi et al., 2007; Lauer et al., 2007, e.g.). A similar correlation, but between M∙M_{\bullet}, re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge}, and ⟨μe,bulge⟩\langle\mu_{\rm e,bulge}\rangle, was reported by Barway & Kembhavi (2007) for nearby ellipticals with measured M∙M_{\bullet}. This correlation has a smaller scatter than the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} and M∙−LbulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{\rm bulge} relations and gives further support to the existence of a FP-type relation for SMBHs.

Furthermore, by comparing the tightness of the correlations between M∙M_{\bullet} and linear combination of the bulge parameters, we argue that σe\sigma_{\rm e} is the parameter that drives the connection with M∙M_{\bullet} in the BHFP. A small contribution is due to re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} or Li,bulgeL_{i,{\rm bulge}}. Similar results were obtained by Aller & Richstone (2007) who compared M∙M_{\bullet} with σe\sigma_{\rm e}, Ie,bulgeI_{\rm e,bulge} and re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge}. Thus, including an additional parameter to the relation does not improve the quality of the fit, with σe\sigma_{\rm e} always being the dominant parameter.

4.2.2 M∙M_{\bullet} versus Galaxy Parameters

We also wish to test if the shallow M∙−Li,galM_{\bullet}-L_{i,{\rm gal}} and M∙M_{\bullet}−-M⋆,galM_{\star,\rm gal} relations can be improved by the addition of another galaxy parameter. Therefore, we calculated the residuals of M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e}, M∙−Li,galM_{\bullet}-L_{i,{\rm gal}}, and M∙M_{\bullet}−-M⋆,galM_{\star,\rm gal} relations to look for the signature of an additional galaxy parameter. The residuals were obtained as the difference between the data points and the relation fits listed in Table 5. We compared the residuals in log⁡(M∙/M∙​[σe])\log(M_{\bullet}/M_{\bullet}[\sigma_{\rm e}]), log⁡(M∙/M∙​[Li,gal])\log(M_{\bullet}/M_{\bullet}[L_{i,{\rm gal}}]), and log⁡(M∙/M∙​[M⋆,gal])\log(M_{\bullet}/M_{\bullet}[M_{\star,\rm gal}]) with the galaxy photometric and kinematic properties (i.e., C28C_{28}, Ie,galI_{\rm e,gal}, re,galr_{\rm e,gal}, and σe\sigma_{\rm e}; Figure 17). For log⁡(M∙/M∙​[σe])\log(M_{\bullet}/M_{\bullet}[\sigma_{\rm e}]), no trends with other galaxy properties are found whereas the log⁡(M∙/M∙​[Li,gal])\log(M_{\bullet}/M_{\bullet}[L_{i,{\rm gal}}]) and log⁡(M∙/M∙​[M⋆,gal])\log(M_{\bullet}/M_{\bullet}[M_{\star,\rm gal}]) relations show a weak dependence on rer_{\rm e} according to the Spearman rank correlation coefficient with a significance levels of 0.3% and 0.9%, respectively. We also examined the residuals of the M∙M_{\bullet}−(g−i)-(g-i) relation to check that our results are not affected by the propagated errors in the determination of M⋆,galM_{\star,\rm gal}. Figure 18 shows the different linear combinations of two galaxy parameters with M∙M_{\bullet}. A few tight correlations are found when considering the total galaxy rather than bulge parameters. The tightness always depends on having σe\sigma_{\rm e} as a fitting parameter (Table 6), i.e., the Spearman rank correlation coefficient is higher when σe\sigma_{\rm e} is taken into account. The constancy of the Spearman rank correlation coefficient despite the addition of other fitting parameters, argues that the main acting parameter is σe\sigma_{\rm e}.

We conclude that the addition of bulge (e.g., re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge}, Li,bulgeL_{i,{\rm bulge}}, MbulgeM_{\rm bulge}) or galaxy (e.g., re,galr_{\rm e,gal}, Li,galL_{i,{\rm gal}}, M⋆,galM_{\star,\rm gal}) structural parameters does not appreciably modify and improve the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation. We exclude that parameter covariances would produce the same scatter in both the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} and M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e}−-rer_{\rm e} relations. Such a conspiracy would require an anti-correlation between σe\sigma_{\rm e} and re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} (or re,galr_{\rm e,gal}) which is not observed.

5 Discussion

The existence of the M∙M_{\bullet} scaling relations implies that SMBH and galaxy formation processes are closely linked. Some of the challenges of the current models of SMBH formation and evolution include reproducing and maintaining the relations regardless of the sequence of galaxy evolution during the hierarchical mass assembly (Robertson et al., 2006a; Schawinski et al., 2006; Croton, 2009). A more comprehensive assessment the M∙M_{\bullet} scaling relations scatter thus enables a better characterisation of the different SMBH/galaxy formation models.

Our large sample of galaxies with secure determination or upper limits of M∙M_{\bullet} has enabled a thorough investigation of the SMBH demography over a wide range of M∙M_{\bullet}, morphological type, and nuclear activity. After establishing the unbiased mapping of M∙M_{\bullet} upper limits against that of secure M∙M_{\bullet}, we tested whether M∙M_{\bullet} is more fundamentally driven by one of the several bulge (i.e., the velocity dispersion, luminosity, virial mass, Sérsic index, and mean effective surface brightness) and galaxy (luminosity, circular velocity, stellar, virial, and dynamical mass) parameters known to correlate with the SMBH mass, and if the known scaling relations can be improved with the addition of a third parameter.

  • •

    We argue that M∙M_{\bullet} is fundamentally driven by σe\sigma_{\rm e}, considering that the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation has the tightest scatter with respect to all other scaling relations. The scatter of our M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation is comparable to 66 but slightly larger than that of Ferrarese & Ford (2005). At small σe\sigma_{\rm e}, some M∙M_{\bullet} upper limits exceed the expectation value as they likely account for the mass of a conspicuous nuclear cluster (12). Excluding these galaxies from the fit reduces the scatter to Ferrarese & Ford (2005)’s value. Barred and unbarred galaxies as in 12 and 66 follow the same M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation within the errors, contrary to Graham (2008)’s findings. Classical and pseudo-bulges were identified according to their Sérsic index (Kormendy & Kennicutt, 2004). The M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relations of classical and pseudo-bulges have a different slope. The low significance of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation for pseudo-bulges is in agreement with more recent findings by Kormendy et al. (2011) and suggests that the formation and growth histories of SMBHs depend on the host bulge type.

  • •

    The M∙−Li,bulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{i,{\rm bulge}} relation is clearly not as tight as the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} one. However, the fact that 66 found a M∙−Li,bulgeM_{\bullet}-L_{i,{\rm bulge}} relation as tight as the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} one is not in contradiction with our results, since 66 accounted only for early-type galaxies. The same is true for the M∙−MbulgeM_{\bullet}-M_{\rm bulge} correlation, although the bulge mass proved to be a better proxy of M∙M_{\bullet} than LbulgeL_{\rm bulge} and it includes re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} as an additional fitting parameter.

  • •

    Contrary to previous findings (Graham et al., 2001; Graham et al., 2003; Graham & Driver, 2007), we find little or no correlation between M∙M_{\bullet} and Sérsic nn in agreement with Hopkins et al. (2007b). The latter stated that M∙M_{\bullet} is unrelated with the light concentration of the bulge based on observations and simulations. Consistently, we confirm that M∙M_{\bullet} and ⟨μe,bulge⟩\langle\mu_{\rm e,bulge}\rangle are poorly correlated.

  • •

    The correlations between M∙M_{\bullet} and galaxy luminosity or mass are not a marked improvement over the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation. These scaling relations are strongly sensitive to the morphology of the host galaxies, with the presence of a disc playing an anti-correlating rôle, as first pointed out by (Kormendy, 2001). This is a further indication that bulges are driving the SMBH correlations and SMBH evolution.

  • •

    We found that the M∙M_{\bullet}−-VcV_{\rm c} relation is significantly coarser than that of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation, with a scatter about twice larger, suggesting that M∙M_{\bullet} is more strongly controlled by the baryons than the dark matter.

  • •

    To assess the need for an additional parameter in the M∙M_{\bullet}-bulge/galaxy scaling relations, we performed both a residual analysis and third-parameter fits as in Hopkins et al. (2007b), Barway & Kembhavi (2007), and Aller & Richstone (2007). To this aim we considered different linear combinations of bulge or galaxy parameters with M∙M_{\bullet}. The strongest correlations always include σe\sigma_{\rm e} as a fundamental structural parameter. The tightest relation is found between M∙M_{\bullet}, σe\sigma_{\rm e}, and re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} (also known as the BHFP, Hopkins et al. 2007a; Hopkins et al. 2007b). Since its scatter does not change appreciably compared to that of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation, the addition of re,bulger_{\rm e,bulge} is barely an improvement. This is a further confirmation that σe\sigma_{\rm e} is the fundamental parameter which drives also the BHFP.

Our findings about the tightness of scaling relations such as the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} may be interpreted in the framework of self-regulating feedback in galaxies Hopkins et al. (2009). These authors argued that the energy released from the accretion of gas onto a SMBH is enough to stop further gas accretion, drive away the gas, and quench star formation. Hopkins et al. (2009) studied the relation between M∙M_{\bullet} and the mass of the gas accreting onto the SMBH as a function of the distance from the central engine. The scatter of the M∙M_{\bullet}-stellar mass relation increases at smaller radii (i.e., approaching the radius of influence of the SMBH) and decreases at larger radii (i.e., where the SMBH scaling relations are defined). This has been interpreted in terms of self-regulated growth of SMBHs, where the SMBH accretes and regulates itself without accounting for the gas supply but just being controlled by the bulge properties.

In this scenario, σe\sigma_{\rm e} is the property which gives the tightest connection with MBH since it determines the depth of the local potential well from which the gas must be expelled. Younger et al. (2008) studied self-regulated models of SMBHs growth in different scenarios of major mergers, minor mergers, and disc instabilities, to find that SMBHs depend on the scale at which self-regulation occurs. They compared the bulge binding energy and total binding energy with M∙M_{\bullet}, finding that the total binding energy is not a good indicator of M∙M_{\bullet} mass in disc-dominated systems. This agrees with our findings that the late-type systems deviate most significantly from the M∙M_{\bullet}-galaxy and BHFP scaling relations.

Several SMBH formation models predict a connection between M∙M_{\bullet} and the total mass of the galaxy (Haehnelt et al., 1998; Silk & Rees, 1998; Adams et al., 2001; Croton et al., 2006; Croton, 2009) such that if the dark and baryonic matter act to form the bulge and SMBH, the dark halo determines the bulge and SMBH properties. Therefore, the mass of the SMBH and dark matter halo should be connected (Cattaneo, 2001; Hopkins et al., 2005a; Hopkins et al., 2005b). Numerous recent studies have erred along those lines. For instance, Bandara et al. (2009) studied the correlation between M∙M_{\bullet} and total (luminous+dark) mass of the galaxy estimated from numerical simulations of gravitational lensing. Their relation suggests that the more massive halos are more efficient at forming SMBHs than the less massive ones; the slope of their relation suggests merger-driven, feedback-regulated processes of SMBH growth. Likewise, Booth & Schaye (2010) used self-consistent simulations of the coevolution of SMBHs and galaxies to confirm the relation by Bandara et al. (2009) and to prove that self-regulation of the SMBH growth occurs on dark matter halo scales. Volonteri & Natarajan (2009) investigated through numerical simulations the observational signature of the self-regulated SMBH growth by analysing the mass assembly history of black hole seeds. They found that the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation stems from the merging history of massive dark halos, and that its slope and scatter depend on the halo seed and specific SMBH self-regulation process.

Our observational results are not supportive of such results. We found only a weak correlation of M∙M_{\bullet} with VcV_{\rm c}. This agrees with our expectations based on the observed tightness of the M∙−σeM_{\bullet}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation and given the fact that the scatter of the Vc−σeV_{\rm c}-\sigma_{\rm e} relation is large and morphologically-dependent (Courteau et al., 2007; Ho, 2007).

The M∙M_{\bullet}-VcV_{\rm c} relation may be improved with homogeneous measurements of the VcV_{\rm c} data base. Indeed, while our collection of observed velocities is as current and reliable as possible, especially for spiral galaxies, we still lack a fully homogeneous data base. Many of us are working on improvements of this nefarious situation. However it is clear, as this work demonstrates, that the M∙M_{\bullet}-σ\sigma is the definitive fundamental relation of the SMBH-bulge connection.

The nuclear spectral class of galaxies marked with * is from the NASA/IPAC Extragalactic Database (NED). Col.(4): distance. All the distances were taken from the literature except those we obtained from V3​KV_{\rm 3K} the weighted mean recessional velocity corrected to the reference frame of the microwave background radiation given in RC3. These were derived as D=V3​K/H0D=V_{\rm 3K}/H_{0} with and H0=70H_{0}=70 km s-1 Mpc-1. For M∙M_{\bullet} upper limits of 66 we adopted the distances from their paper. Col.(5): References for Col.(4). Col.(6): Absolute corrected BB magnitude derived from BT0B^{0}_{T} (RC3) with the adopted distance. The value of UGC 1841 reported by 12 has been corrected adopting the effective radius by Donzelli et al. (2007). Col.(8): Inclination of the disc galaxies derived from either the fitted disc axial ratio (from this paper) or the isophotal axial ratio at a surface brightness of μB=25\mu_{B}=25 mag arcsec-2 (from RC3) and the intrinsic disc axial ratio (derived following Paturel et al. (1997)). Col.(9): References for the apparent axial ratio adopted to calculate the inclination given in Col.(8). Col.(10): Circular velocity. The circular velocities were derived from either H i line-width measurements or gas resolved kinematics available in literature corrected according to the adopted inclination. Only the values marked with * are from dynamical models of the stellar component. Col.(11): References for Col.(10). Col.(5): Ellipticity of the isophotes. Col.(6): Integrated ii-band magnitude within the isophote at a surface brightness level of 24.5 mag arcsec-2 corrected for Galactic extinction, K-correction, and internal extinction following (Shao et al., 2007). Col.(7): Radius of isophote at a surface brightness level of μi=24.5\mu_{i}=24.5 mag arcsec-2. Col.(8): Effective surface brightness of the galaxy. Col.(9): Effective radius of the galaxy. Col.(10): Concentration index C28=5​log⁡(r80/r20)C_{28}=5\log(r_{80}/r_{20}) where r80r_{80} and r20r_{20} are the radii that enclose 80% and 20% of total light, respectively.

Notes. — Col.(1): Galaxy name. Col.(2): Result of the two dimensional decomposition of the galaxy surface brightness distribution: yes = successful fit; no = unsuccessful fit; Col.(3): Comments about the fit: r1/nr^{1/n} = the galaxy has been successfully fitted with a Sérsic law; r1/n+r^{1/n}+exp. = the galaxy has been successfully fitted with a Sérsic bulge and exponential disc; bad = inadequate one or two-component fit; Freeman II disc = the disc seems to follow a Freeman Type II law; embedded disc = the bulge and disc components have been fitted with a Sérsic and exponential law, respectively. But, the bulge is dominating the light contribution at both small and large radii; bar = a strong bar is present in addition to the bulge and disc components; light excess = the light excess measured at large radii can not be parametrised with an exponential function. A cut-off profile (Oemler, 1976, e.g.,) is required.

Col.(4): Effective surface brightness of the bulge. Col.(5): Effective radius of the bulge. Col.(6): Shape parameter of the bulge. Col.(7): Axial ratio of the bulge isophotes. Col.(8): Position angle of the bulge major-axis. Col.(9): Central surface brightness of the disc. Col.(10): Scale length of the disc. Col.(11): Axial ratio of the disc isophotes. Col.(12): Position angle of the disc major-axis. Col.(13): Bulge-to-total luminosity ratio. Col.(14): Total magnitude of the bulge.
